title: You did not throw
hook: at Badr, you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw (8:17)
tomorrow: Between a man and his heart

segments.voice: Yesterday: wajilat, hearts that tremble. Your line was a heart that trembles. What moved yours? Today, still at Badr, a verse about who gets the credit. Day four hundred seventeen.

An award show. The winner gets to the microphone and starts thanking people. My coach, my mom, the team, the crew. Some of it is politeness. But there's often something true in it: they know the trophy has their name on it, and they also know it was never only them. At Badr, the sources say, the Muslims were badly outnumbered. Commentators report that as the battle began, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ picked up a handful of pebbles and dust and threw it toward the other army. And afterward, a verse came about that throw.
screen: `THE ACCEPTANCE SPEECH.` → `OUTNUMBERED AT BADR.` → `A HANDFUL OF PEBBLES.`

segments.voice: Verse seventeen begins with the believers: you did not slay them, but Allah slew them. Then it turns to the Prophet, in Pickthall's words: “thou (Muhammad) threwest not when thou didst throw, but Allah threw.” In Arabic it's almost a riddle: wa ma ramayta idh ramayta, wa lakinna Allaha rama. You did not throw, when you threw. The verse doesn't deny that the Prophet's arm moved. It says, you threw, and in the same breath: it wasn't you. In the verse's telling, both are true at once. The hand was his; the reaching of that handful, and what came of it, was Allah's. The verse goes on: that He might test the believers with a good test from Him. Even the victory is a test: what will you do with it? Will you say, look at us? Remember yesterday: the surah opened with an argument over the spoils. This verse quietly answers that argument. If the win wasn't only yours, the spoils aren't only yours either. Muslim theologians have long argued over this verse, asking how a human act can be both truly yours and truly from God. Different schools gave different answers, and the debate is still taught. The everyday lesson teachers draw is simpler. Effort is real, and it matters. Success is a gift, and it humbles. After good news, a job, a grade, a recovery, Muslims say alhamdulillah, praise be to God. In a way, it's this verse, in one word.
screen: `WA MA RAMAYTA — YOU DID NOT THROW.` · `THE HAND WAS HIS; THE REST, ALLAH'S.` · `EVEN VICTORY IS A TEST.` · `EFFORT REAL, SUCCESS A GIFT.` · then, large: `BUT ALLAH THREW.`

segments.voice: Sit, and breathe. Think of one thing you're proud of, from this week or this year: something that worked, something you finished, someone you helped. Let yourself feel the effort you put in. It was real. Then widen the picture: the health that let you do it, the people who taught you, the timing you didn't control, the breath in your lungs. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for it. If not, simply credit what wasn't you. The bell holds the time.
Rama, threw. Surah eight, verse seventeen: you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw. The hand was the Prophet's; the outcome was Allah's. Today's word.
Your line: it wasn't only me. Today, when something goes well, name out loud one thing that wasn't you, and one person who helped. Day four hundred seventeen.

fork.setup: you've just won against the odds. everyone's congratulating you. what does 8:17 point you toward?
options: take full credit. you earned it.
own the effort, and credit Allah for the outcome.
say you did nothing at all.
fork.reveal: you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw: the act was real, and the outcome a gift and a test.

original.note: Arabic: and you did not throw when you threw (8:17).

trapdoor: what you thought: God helped win a battle.
what it means: human effort is real, and the outcome belongs to Allah; even a victory is a test.
what a scholar hears: 8:17 is a classic proof-text in debates on human acts: Ash'aris cite it for divine creation of acts with human acquisition (kasb); Sufis read it as tawhid of action.
